questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Albendazole acts by:
options: Binding beta-tubulin and inhibiting microtubule polymerisation in the parasite
questions.concept: Selective toxicity arises from higher affinity for parasite tubulin. Albendazole covers most intestinal nematodes and is used with praziquantel for neurocysticercosis and for hydatid disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Ivermectin acts by:
options: Opening glutamate-gated chloride channels causing parasite paralysis
questions.concept: These channels are absent in mammals and ivermectin poorly crosses the intact blood-brain barrier, giving selective toxicity. It is the drug of choice for strongyloidiasis, onchocerciasis and crusted scabies.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Diethylcarbamazine remains the mainstay for lymphatic filariasis and is given with albendazole because:
options: The combination improves clearance of microfilariae in mass drug administration
questions.concept: Mass drug administration with DEC plus albendazole, or ivermectin-based triple therapy, aims to interrupt transmission. The Mazzotti reaction from dying microfilariae limits DEC use in onchocerciasis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Multidrug therapy for multibacillary leprosy comprises:
options: Rifampicin, clofazimine and dapsone for 12 months
questions.concept: Monthly supervised rifampicin and clofazimine with daily clofazimine and dapsone is given for 12 months in multibacillary and 6 months of rifampicin and dapsone in paucibacillary disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: The most important adverse effect of dapsone is:
options: Haemolysis, particularly severe in G6PD deficiency, and methaemoglobinaemia
questions.concept: Dapsone also causes agranulocytosis and the dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome. It is additionally used for dermatitis herpetiformis and Pneumocystis prophylaxis in sulfa-intolerant patients.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Clofazimine characteristically causes:
questions.concept: The pigmentation is dose-related and reversible but distressing, a major cause of poor adherence. Clofazimine also has anti-inflammatory action valuable in erythema nodosum leprosum.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: The drug of choice for invasive amoebiasis including amoebic liver abscess is:
options: Metronidazole followed by a luminal amoebicide
questions.concept: Metronidazole clears tissue trophozoites but not luminal cysts, so a luminal agent such as diloxanide furoate or paromomycin must follow to prevent relapse and further transmission.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Metronidazole with alcohol causes:
options: A disulfiram-like reaction with flushing, vomiting and headache
questions.concept: Inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase causes acetaldehyde accumulation, so alcohol is avoided during and for 48 hours after therapy. Metronidazole also potentiates warfarin and causes a metallic taste and peripheral neuropathy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Erythema nodosum leprosum (type 2 lepra reaction) is best treated with:
options: Thalidomide, or corticosteroids where thalidomide is contraindicated
questions.concept: Thalidomide is dramatically effective but absolutely contraindicated in women of childbearing potential because of phocomelia. Multidrug therapy is continued throughout the reaction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Praziquantel is the drug of choice for:
options: Schistosomiasis and most cestode infections including taeniasis
questions.concept: It increases parasite membrane permeability to calcium causing tetanic paralysis and tegumental damage. In neurocysticercosis it is used with albendazole and corticosteroids to control inflammation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Ciclosporin acts by:
options: Inhibiting calcineurin and thereby IL-2 production by T cells
questions.concept: Ciclosporin binds cyclophilin and tacrolimus binds FKBP, both inhibiting calcineurin. Nephrotoxicity is dose-limiting and requires trough level monitoring; gum hypertrophy and hirsutism are characteristic of ciclosporin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Azathioprine dose must be reduced when given with allopurinol because:
options: Xanthine oxidase inhibition prevents metabolism of its active metabolite, causing marrow suppression
questions.concept: Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine which is degraded by xanthine oxidase; blocking this enzyme leads to accumulation and severe myelosuppression, so the dose is cut to about a quarter.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Methotrexate toxicity is reduced by:
options: Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue and weekly rather than daily dosing
questions.concept: Folinic acid bypasses the blocked dihydrofolate reductase step rescuing normal cells. A catastrophic error is daily instead of weekly dosing in rheumatoid arthritis, causing fatal mucositis and marrow aplasia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Before starting anti-TNF biologicals such as infliximab, it is essential to screen for:
questions.concept: TNF is essential for maintaining granulomas, so blockade reactivates latent tuberculosis, often in disseminated or extrapulmonary form. Screening with tuberculin test or IGRA and chest radiograph is mandatory.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Cyclophosphamide characteristically causes haemorrhagic cystitis, prevented by:
questions.concept: The metabolite acrolein irritates the bladder urothelium; mesna binds it in urine. Cyclophosphamide also causes marrow suppression, infertility, alopecia, SIADH and later bladder carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of:
options: Clotting factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S
questions.concept: Deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time first because factor VII has the shortest half-life. Newborns receive prophylactic vitamin K because of low stores, sterile gut and low content in breast milk.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Vitamin A in very high doses during early pregnancy is:
options: Teratogenic, causing craniofacial and cardiac defects
questions.concept: Retinoids including isotretinoin and acitretin are potent teratogens, requiring strict contraception. Chronic hypervitaminosis A also causes benign intracranial hypertension, bone pain and hepatotoxicity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: The chelating agent of choice for lead poisoning in a child with encephalopathy is:
options: Calcium disodium edetate, often with dimercaprol
questions.concept: Severe lead poisoning is treated with parenteral edetate plus dimercaprol, given first to avoid redistributing lead to the brain. Succimer is used orally for less severe poisoning.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Penicillamine is used in Wilson disease because it:
questions.concept: Pyridoxine is co-administered as penicillamine is an antipyridoxine agent. Trientine is an alternative chelator and zinc blocks intestinal copper absorption, used for maintenance therapy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody directed against:
questions.concept: B-cell depletion is used in non-Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, rheumatoid arthritis, ANCA vasculitis and pemphigus. Hepatitis B reactivation and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy are recognised risks.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, prescription writing & drug schedules
questions.stem: Phase I clinical trials are primarily designed to assess:
options: Safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics, usually in healthy volunteers
questions.concept: Phase I involves 20 to 100 subjects; phase II assesses efficacy and dose-finding in a few hundred patients; phase III confirms efficacy in large randomised trials; and phase IV is post-marketing surveillance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, prescription writing & drug schedules
questions.stem: Randomisation in a clinical trial is performed to:
options: Eliminate selection bias and balance known and unknown confounders between groups
questions.concept: Randomisation is the only method that balances unmeasured confounders, which is why randomised controlled trials sit at the top of the evidence hierarchy. Allocation concealment protects the randomisation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, prescription writing & drug schedules
questions.stem: A double-blind trial means that:
options: Neither the participant nor the investigator knows the treatment allocation
questions.concept: Blinding minimises performance and detection bias, particularly important for subjective outcomes such as pain. Where blinding is impossible, blinded outcome assessment is used instead.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, prescription writing & drug schedules
questions.stem: An intention-to-treat analysis means:
options: Participants are analysed in the group to which they were randomised, regardless of adherence
Groups are reassigned by treatment received
questions.concept: ITT preserves the benefits of randomisation and gives a pragmatic estimate of effectiveness. Per-protocol analysis, which excludes non-adherers, reintroduces selection bias and typically overestimates efficacy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, prescription writing & drug schedules
questions.stem: Pharmacovigilance is defined as:
options: The science of detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse drug effects
questions.concept: Spontaneous reporting under the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India detects rare adverse effects missed in trials of limited size and duration. Under-reporting is the main weakness of such systems.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, prescription writing & drug schedules
questions.stem: A type A adverse drug reaction is:
options: Dose-related and predictable from the drug's pharmacology, such as bleeding with warfarin
questions.concept: Type A (augmented) reactions are common, predictable and dose-dependent and are managed by dose reduction. Type B (bizarre) reactions are unpredictable, often immunological and usually require drug withdrawal.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, prescription writing & drug schedules
questions.stem: Schedule H drugs under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules are those which:
options: Can be sold only on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner
questions.concept: Schedule H and H1 require prescription, with H1 additionally requiring the pharmacist to keep a separate register for three years - a measure aimed at curbing antimicrobial misuse and resistance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, prescription writing & drug schedules
questions.stem: Schedule X drugs differ from Schedule H in that they:
options: Require a prescription in duplicate, with the pharmacist retaining a copy for two years
questions.concept: Schedule X covers drugs with high abuse potential such as certain barbiturates and amphetamines, with stringent record-keeping and storage requirements under lock and key.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, prescription writing & drug schedules
questions.stem: The essential parts of a prescription include the superscription, inscription, subscription and:
options: Signatura (directions to the patient), with the prescriber's signature and registration number
questions.concept: Legible writing, generic names, avoidance of dangerous abbreviations such as U for units, and clear dose and duration reduce medication errors, which are a major preventable source of patient harm.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, prescription writing & drug schedules
questions.stem: An essential medicines list is defined by WHO as drugs that:
options: Satisfy the priority health care needs of the population, selected for efficacy, safety and cost-effectiveness
questions.concept: The concept promotes rational prescribing and procurement. India's National List of Essential Medicines also underpins price control, improving affordability and access.
